papers.title_in_file: FiFAR: A Fraud Detection Dataset for Learning to Defer
papers.not_read: The Appendix (including section D and Table 6, which the main text cites) is not in the text layer; the text ends at the reference list. Equations in Section 3.2 are garbled glyphs in the text layer and were not read as formulas.
papers.what_it_is: A dataset paper that introduces FiFAR, a synthetic bank account fraud dataset with the predictions of 50 synthetic fraud analysts and capacity constraints, plus three capacity-aware deferral baselines tested under 300 scenarios.

quotes: The main limitation of our work is that our baselines do not include any established methods in the L2D literature, as these do not currently consider the existence of capacity constraints.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the limit of the authors' own baselines.

existing.note: The 'throughout all the considered scenarios' statement is made about the main baseline results table. The paper's table that varies the expert pool says ReLlinear outperforms ReL when the pool holds only agreeing, sparse or unfair experts. The stored value omits this.
existing.value: The authors report that, throughout all the considered scenarios of the main baseline results, rejection learning performs best, despite their attempts to model human behavior; they also report that, when the expert pool contains only agreeing, sparse or unfair experts, ReLlinear outperforms ReL; they provide three L2D baselines tested under 300 different scenarios.
quotes: We observe that, throughout all the considered scenarios, rejection learning performs best, despite our attempts to model human behavior.
Here we can see that ReLlinear outperforms ReL when the expert pool contains only agreeing, sparse or unfair experts.
we provide three L2D baselines tested under 300 different scenarios.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on synthetic experts.
existing.reader_inference: In the paper's own Section 2.3, rejection learning is separate from learning to defer, yet Section 5 calls all three baselines L2D baselines. Lower loss is better, so the second table's lower ReLlinear losses in the three pools back the narrowing.

quotes: we introduce the Financial Fraud Alert Review Dataset (FiFAR), a synthetic bank account fraud detection dataset, containing the predictions of a team of 50 highly complex and varied synthetic fraud analysts
As the base dataset, we choose to use the publicly available bankaccount-fraud tabular dataset [23].
The data was generated by applying tabular data generation techniques on an anonymized, real-world bank account opening fraud detection dataset.
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract and Section 3.1 state the dataset's own setup.

quotes: We emphasize that our synthetic experts can not replace, in any way, humans involved in HAIC systems
our synthetic experts may amplify biases
existing.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the limits of the authors' own synthetic experts.

assertions.value: The authors state that public dataset limitations have significantly hindered the development and benchmarking of learning to defer algorithms, and that there are no publicly available datasets for L2D concerning financial fraud detection.
quotes: Public dataset limitations have significantly hindered the development and benchmarking of learning to defer (L2D) algorithms
there are no publicly available datasets for L2D concerning this important application of human-AI teaming
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the state of the field, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the NIH Clinical Center X-ray dataset has predictions from an ensemble of 22 experts and a golden label from an independent team of 3 radiologists, and that its main drawback is its size of 4,374 X-ray images.
quotes: there are recorded predictions from an ensemble of 22 experts, and a golden label created by an independent team of 3 radiologists
it contains only 4,374 X-ray images
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another group's dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Hate Speech and Offensive Language Detection dataset as enriched by Keswani et al. has 1,471 tweets annotated by a total of 170 crowd-sourcing workers, an average of 10 workers per tweet and an average of 87 instances per worker.
quotes: consists of a subset of 1,471 tweets from the original dataset [10], annotated by a total of 170 crowd-sourcing workers
Each tweet was labelled by an average of 10 workers, meaning that each worker labelled an average of 87 instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another group's dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not use the model-as-expert approach to simulate experts because it may lead to artificially large agreement between the classifier and the experts, and that they use instance-dependent label noise instead.
quotes: This may lead to artificially large agreement between the classifier and experts, which is why we choose not to use it.
Our approach will make use of instance-dependent label noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2.2 states the authors' own design choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the FiFAR dataset has three components: a base dataset with each instance's features, a table of each synthetic expert's predictions for each instance, and a set of capacity constraints; they also create a version simulating realistic data availability with only one expert prediction per instance during training.
quotes: The FiFAR Dataset is comprised by three components
We also create a version of our dataset simulating realistic data availability conditions (only one expert prediction per instance) during training
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 1 and 3 state the dataset's own makeup.

assertions.value: The authors state that each instance is a bank account opening application, that a positive prediction results in a declined application, and that the optimization goal is to maximize recall at a fixed FPR of 5%, which implicitly establishes a relationship between the costs of false positives and false negatives.
quotes: Each instance represents a bank account opening application
A positive prediction results in a declined application.
The optimization goal is to maximize recall at a fixed FPR (we use 5%), which implicitly establishes a relationship between the costs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 states the task and goal the paper uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that ML models trained on the base dataset tend to raise more false fraud alerts for older clients (at least 50 years old), reducing their access to a bank account.
quotes: ML models trained on this dataset tend to raise more false fraud alerts for older clients (≥ 50 years), thus reducing their access to a bank account.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement given without a measurement in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their expert generation is based on instance-dependent noise: synthetic predictions are made by flipping each label with a probability that depends on the instance's features and, optionally, on the model score; the weight vector embodies a relation between the features and the probability of error, and the weights are normalized so that the overall magnitude of variation can be controlled separately.
quotes: Our expert generation approach is based on instance-dependent noise
We generate synthetic predictions by flipping each label
The weight vector w embodies a relation between the features and the probability of error.
The feature weights are normalized so that we can separately control, with the
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 defines the generator; the formulas are not legible in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that they created four distinct expert groups (Standard, Unfair, Model agreeing, Sparse), that all groups have similar performance as measured by TPR and FPR with a fraction of the team performing worse than the ML model, and that the Standard group is on average as unfair as the model, dependent on model score and on average on twelve different features.
quotes: we created four distinct expert groups. All groups have similar performance as measured by their TPR and FPR, with a fraction of the team performing worse than the ML Model.
on average as unfair as the model, dependent on model score and, on average, twelve different features.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3 states how the authors built their expert team.

assertions.value: The authors define capacity constraints by a batch vector and a capacity matrix whose entries are non-negative integers giving the number of instances each expert can process in each batch, set by 4 parameters: deferral rate, a homogeneous or variable distribution of capacity, absence rate, and expert pool.
quotes: we consider 4 separate parameters. (1) Deferral_rate: maximum fraction of each batch that can be deferred to the human team
Absence rate, defined as the fraction of experts that are absent in each batch.
Expert Pool, defined as which types of experts (standard, unfair, sparse or model agreeing) can be part of the team.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.4 defines the paper's capacity constraints.

assertions.value: The authors state that the fraud model, a LightGBM classifier, is trained on the first three months of the dataset and validated on the fourth month, with a recall of 57.9% in validation at a threshold chosen to obtain 5% FPR; the simulated experts act from the fourth to the eighth month, and the assignment algorithms are trained on months four to six and validated on the seventh month.
quotes: This model is trained on the first three months of the dataset and validated on the fourth month.
The ML model yields a recall of 57.9% in validation
chosen in validation to obtain 5% FPR.
we train our assignment algorithms with the data of months four to six, validating them on the seventh month.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.5 states the experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that, without an assignment method, the decision system works as follows: a batch is processed by the model, a fraction of the highest scoring instances is flagged for human review and randomly assigned to experts, and the rest of the instances are automatically accepted.
quotes: a fraction of the highest scoring instances are flagged for human review, and, finally, these instances are randomly assigned to experts, who make the final decision. The rest of the instances are automatically accepted.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.5 states the review workflow the paper simulates.

assertions.value: The authors evaluate assignments with a cost-sensitive loss that counts false positive errors, weighted by a parameter set from the model's threshold, plus false negative errors, and measure fairness as predictive equality: the FPR of the age group with the lowest observed FPR divided by the FPR of the group with the highest FPR.
quotes: Where N(FP/FN) is the number of FP/FN errors.
we measure the ratio between FPRs in each age group, i.e., predictive equality (PE) [7].
The ratio is calculated by dividing the FPR of the group with lowest observed FPR by the FPR of the group with the highest FPR.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 4.1 and 4.2 define the metrics; Equation 1 is not legible in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that, when searching for possible L2D baselines, they found no current method able to take individual capacity constraints into account, and so provide three baselines.
quotes: When searching for possible L2D baselines, we found no current method able to take individual capacity constraints into account.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the literature, without a systematic search reported.

assertions.value: The authors describe their capacity-aware rejection learning baseline: within each batch, cases are ordered by descending model score, the top 5% are automatically predicted positive, the following cases are randomly assigned to experts until capacity constraints are met, and the remaining lowest-scoring cases are classified negative.
quotes: The top 5% cases are automatically predicted positive (declined).
Then, the following cases are randomly assigned to experts within our team until their capacity constraints are met.
All left over cases, with the lowest model score, are classified negatively (accepted).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 defines the baseline.

assertions.value: The authors describe two human-expertise-aware versions of rejection learning: a LightGBM model is trained on the instance features and the expert id to predict whether the expert's prediction was a false positive, false negative, true positive or true negative; ReLgreedy then assigns each case, in order, to the expert with the lowest predicted loss that still has capacity, and ReLlinear solves an integer linear program that minimizes the predicted loss over the whole batch subject to the capacity constraints.
quotes: we train a LightGBM model on the instance features and the expert_id to predict if the expert
The algorithm moves through the batch case by case, assigning each case to the expert with lowest predicted loss.
we minimize the loss over an entire batch by solving a linear programming problem subject to our capacity constraints
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 defines the two baselines.

assertions.value: The authors report in the first row of their main baseline results table a loss of 918 and predictive equality of 0.33 for the Model Only baseline, and a loss of 753±12 with predictive equality of 0.29 for ReL, 780±10 with 0.31 for ReLgreedy and 780±9 with 0.32 for ReLlinear.
assertions.anchor: Table 1, p.6 (first row: pool all; the column labels are not legible in the text layer)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on synthetic experts.
assertions.reader_inference: Lower loss is better, so ReL (753) beats ReLgreedy and ReLlinear (780) and the Model Only baseline (918) in this row; ReL also has the lowest PE ratio here.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that the expertise-aware methods did not beat rejection learning possibly because of the low volume of false negatives and true positives in the training data, which may lead to poor probability estimates and ranking of the expert's probability of error.
quotes: This may be due to the low volume of FNs and TPs in the training data, which may lead to poor probability estimates and ranking of the expert
assertions.certainty_reason: An untested hypothesis of the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that, according to a table in section D of the Appendix, their expertise-aware methods mostly mitigate false positive errors, giving a lower FPR but also lowering recall, and that the mitigation also leads to higher predictive equality, which they say shows the human expertise model learned that experts make more FP mistakes on older clients' applications.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.3, p.7 (Table 6 is in the Appendix, which is not in the text layer)
quotes: our methods mostly mitigate FP errors, resulting in a lower FPR, but negatively impacting the recall as well.
The mitigation of False Positives also leads to higher predictive equality
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the table that backs it was not available to the reader.
assertions.reader_inference: In the main table the PE of ReLgreedy and ReLlinear (0.31 to 0.37) is above that of ReL (0.29 to 0.30), which fits this claim.

assertions.value: The authors report that for ReLlinear the loss shows no significant effect from expert absence at a 20% deferral rate, but that at a 50% deferral rate introducing expert absence significantly increases the loss, and they say this shows the importance of testing under a wide variety of conditions.
quotes: While it seems that expert absence has no significant effect on the loss for scenarios with a deferral rate of 20%
in the cases with 50% deferral rate, it seems that introducing expert absence significantly increases the loss.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the authors hedge with 'it seems'.
assertions.reader_inference: The column labels of the main table are not legible in the text layer, so the reader did not check this against the table rows.

assertions.value: The authors report that ReLlinear outperforms ReL when the expert pool contains only agreeing, sparse or unfair experts, and suggest this may be because such experts are simpler to model, having a clear dominating feature or simpler feature dependencies.
quotes: Here we can see that ReLlinear outperforms ReL when the expert pool contains only agreeing, sparse or unfair experts.
This may be due to the fact that these experts are simpler to model, as they have a clear dominating feature, or simpler feature dependencies.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, with an untested explanation.
assertions.reader_inference: In the standard pool rows of the second table, ReL has the lower loss (742 against 788 for ReLlinear in the first row), which is consistent with the first table.

assertions.value: The authors report in their expert pool table that in the first unfair pool row ReL, ReLgreedy and ReLlinear have predictive equality of 0.22, 0.24 and 0.25, and in the first standard pool row 0.30, 0.32 and 0.33.
assertions.anchor: Table 2, p.6 (first unfair row and first standard row)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on synthetic experts.
assertions.reader_inference: A lower PE ratio means a larger FPR gap between age groups, so the unfair pool has less equal outcomes than the standard pool, as its design intends.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their dataset enables comprehensive benchmarking of L2D algorithms subject to real world constraints and scenarios.
quotes: Our dataset enables comprehensive benchmarking of L2D algorithms, subject to real world constraints and scenarios.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; no other method is benchmarked on it in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that researchers should prefer real human predictions over synthetic expert predictions where such predictions are accessible and pertinent, and that real expert data would need to be gathered to train a system for real-world use.
quotes: it would be necessary to gather real expert data in order to train the system to be used in a real-world application
In cases where human predictions are accessible and pertinent to the use case, researchers should prefer these over synthetic expert predictions
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the limit on how the synthetic experts may be used.

assertions.value: The authors state that their synthetic experts may amplify biases because they establish a monotonic relationship between each feature and the probabilities of error, so that raising the weight of a feature correlated with the protected attribute could give an expert more bias against the protected group, and they encourage a careful analysis of each expert's final predictive equality.
quotes: due to the fact that they establish a monotonic relationship between each feature and the probabilities of error
a careful analysis of the final predictive equality of each expert is encouraged
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the limit of the authors' own synthetic experts.
